body.text: The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Pekka Virkki – co-founder of Mission Grey, journalist, and author of “Autopsy of Post-Finlandization: The Roots of the European Appeasement of Russia” (ibidem 2026) – is the 536th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Analyze the historical roots of Finlandization and European appeasement of Russia.

Finlandization originated in an extreme asymmetry of power. After the Second World War, Finland was territorially diminished, militarily vulnerable, and exposed to the Soviet Union. The 1948 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance institutionalized this asymmetry without reducing Finland to a full Soviet satellite. Finnish policy sought to avoid confrontation with Moscow while preserving as much sovereignty and domestic autonomy as circumstances permitted.

The crucial development was the transition from external restraint to internal self-restraint. Political leaders, officials, businesses, and parts of the media increasingly anticipated Soviet reactions. Soviet influence was reinforced by networks of agents of influence and informal contacts. Formal democratic institutions survived, but the range of politically feasible choices narrowed.

Post-Cold War European accommodation of Russia arose under different circumstances but reproduced comparable mechanisms: confidence that economic interdependence would moderate Russian behavior, growing energy dependence, elite networks linked to Russian interests, and repeated discounting of warning signs, particularly after the wars in Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine from 2014. These factors reinforced one another. Commercial incentives and the immediate costs of confrontation repeatedly favored accommodation despite mounting strategic risks, ultimately paving the way for renewed Russian aggression against Ukraine in 2022.

The broader lesson is one of path dependence. Finlandization does not mean a rapid, explicit surrender of sovereignty, but it develops through individually defensible compromises – selective silence, exceptional arrangements, economic normalization, and delayed responses – which progressively lower the threshold for further accommodation.
Describe what a plausible scenario of the Finlandization of Taiwan would look like.

Finlandization has periodically been proposed as a solution to Taiwan’s security dilemma. Bruce Gilley’s 2010 argument exemplified a liberal-internationalist version: economic integration, political interaction, and accommodation could reduce conflict and potentially socialize, even liberalize, China. This resembles assumptions that also informed parts of Europe’s post-Cold War Russia policy.

A contemporary Finlandization scenario would probably be more coercive and incremental. It would not initially entail annexation or “one country, two systems.” Taiwan could retain elections, armed forces, democratic institutions, and de facto self-government while gradually losing strategic freedom of action.

The process could proceed through four stages. First, persistent Chinese military, maritime, cyber, economic, informational, and legal pressure normalizes coercion below the threshold of war. Second, Taiwan’s partners increasingly prioritize crisis management, encouraging Taipei to exercise restraint. Third, external restraint becomes internalized: Taiwanese political and economic elites advocate reduced defense visibility, softer sovereignty rhetoric, closer economic relations with China, and limitations on foreign security cooperation. Finally, Beijing acquires an informal veto over politically feasible Taiwanese choices without directly governing Taiwan.
The paradoxical endpoint would be a scenario where Taiwan remains democratic but is no longer fully strategically autonomous.

There is, however, no guarantee that democracy and accommodation would remain confined within these limits. Concessions do not in themselves preclude further demands, or ultimately even military aggression. From the Soviet perspective, this was also part of the logic of Finlandization: “peaceful coexistence as an instrument of class struggle.” Finnish interpretations tended to retain the “peaceful coexistence” while conveniently leaving out its Soviet qualifier: “as an instrument of class struggle.”
What domestic conditions would cause the Finlandization of Taiwan?

The most important domestic condition would be a loss of confidence in the utility of resistance. Accommodation becomes politically attractive if substantial parts of Taiwanese society conclude that resisting China carries unacceptable humanitarian or economic costs while American support cannot ultimately be relied upon.

A second condition would be elite convergence. China-exposed businesses, accommodation-oriented politicians, retired officials, media actors, and local political networks could collectively redefine self-restraint as prudent statecraft rather than capitulation. This would be reinforced by weakened societal capacity to identify covert financing, disinformation, cyber interference, and elite capture.

Economic constituencies would also matter. Mainland-exposed manufacturers, taishang [Taiwanese businesspeople who operate on the mainland] networks, tourism and agricultural interests, and local patronage networks could translate economic losses into demands for political accommodation. They would not need to support unification; it would be sufficient for them to conclude that sustained confrontation is economically intolerable.
What external factors would precipitate the Finlandization of Taiwan?

The principal external driver would be sustained Chinese coercion calibrated below the threshold of war. Beijing would seek to increase the costs of Taiwan exercising its autonomy without creating a clear trigger for external military intervention. PLA operations, coast guard activity, cyber operations, economic coercion, and legal warfare could cumulatively normalize Chinese pressure.

A successful quasi-blockade could constitute a major turning point. Maritime inspections, temporary exclusion zones, customs measures, or “quarantine” arrangements could demonstrate China’s ability to disrupt Taiwanese commerce without provoking an effective international response.

Equally important would be declining confidence in external support. U.S.-China strategic bargaining could implicitly subordinate Taiwan to broader priorities in trade, technology, or bilateral stability. Reduced arms transfers or political contacts would magnify this effect. Regional hedging by Japan, Southeast Asian countries, or European states could further convince Taiwanese actors that their international room for maneuver was contracting.
Identify real-time signals that could indicate the emergence of a Finlandization-of-Taiwan scenario.

No individual indicator would demonstrate Finlandization. The important signal would be convergence across military, international, political, and economic domains. Current trends – high defense expenditure, investment in unmanned and AI capabilities, whole-of-society resilience, and substantial willingness to defend Taiwan – point in the opposite direction. Finlandization would therefore require a reversal across several variables.

The principal indicators would be sustained intensification of Chinese coercion, weakening or increasing ambiguity in U.S. military support and arms deliveries, a shift in Taiwanese political language from deterrence toward reassurance through restraint, and growing advocacy by political and business elites for deeper mainland ties and acceptance of Beijing-defined constraints. Particular attention should be paid to intermediaries capable of translating Chinese preferences into domestically legitimate arguments.

The critical warning sign is therefore not simply more Chinese pressure, but the interaction of prolonged Chinese coercion, allied ambiguity, and Taiwanese domestic adaptation. Finlandization should be understood as a process rather than a predetermined settlement. Its defining threshold is reached when anticipated Chinese reactions begin to constrain Taiwanese choices without Beijing having to impose those constraints directly.
